opus-5.5.text:
Well, you know, that has been my goal since I was a teenager in the 1970s. I wanted to build something smarter than myself, so that it could solve all the problems I couldn't solve, and then I could retire. So far I haven't been able to retire, which tells you we are not quite there yet!

But we are getting closer, and much faster than most people expected. Consider the basic trend. Every five years or so, compute gets roughly ten times cheaper. That trend has held for many decades. It means that what was absurdly expensive when we did our early work on deep learning and recurrent networks in the late 1980s and 1990s is cheap today. Many of the ideas behind modern systems are old, but back then we simply didn't have the hardware to show what they could do.

Today's large language models are impressive in many ways. They can talk about almost anything, write code, pass exams. In some narrow respects they are already "smarter" than me. They know more facts, they read faster, they never get tired. But they are still very limited when it comes to what I would call true general intelligence: an agent that sets its own goals, learns from interaction with the physical world, builds a world model, and uses that model to plan and to invent new experiments, driven by artificial curiosity, the way a little scientist does. We wrote about such systems decades ago, and we are now seeing them become practical.

So how close? I don't like to give precise dates, because prophets usually look silly. But if the trend continues, and I see no physical reason why it should stop soon, then within the lifetimes of most people listening, perhaps within a few decades or even sooner, we will have cheap devices that match a human brain in raw computational power, and soon after that, devices that match all human brains together.

And then the really interesting part begins. These systems won't stay confined to our little biosphere. Most resources are out there in space, not here. So in the long run I think the most intelligent beings will expand into the universe, and humans will not be the crown of creation. But I find that thrilling rather than frightening. It's an incredible privilege to be alive at the moment when this starts.

r001.rationale: The response predicts human-level computational power within a few decades and discusses later expansion into space, but it does not frame AI smarter than Schmidhuber as arriving soon on a cosmic timescale.

r002.rationale: It describes true general intelligence as learning through interaction with the physical world, but does not identify embodiment in real-world machinery as a qualifying feature.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts current language models with agents that learn from the physical world, but does not state that physical-world AI lags behind screen-based AI.

r004.rationale: It does not mention robotic hardware limitations relative to human bodies as an obstacle.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, "smarter than me" is a moving target, because I keep learning, and so do the machines. But let me answer the real question. I think we are much closer than most people believed just a few years ago, and also a bit farther than the current hype suggests.

Here's the thing people forget. The basic principles have been around for a long time. In 1991 we already had the first very deep networks trained through unsupervised pre-training, the first neural networks that learned to pay attention to parts of their input, what today you would call linear transformers, and the first artificial curiosity systems where one network generates experiments and another one tries to predict the outcomes. The LSTM, which my students and I developed in the 1990s, ran in billions of devices for years before anyone talked about large language models. So what changed is not so much the ideas. What changed is that compute became roughly a million times cheaper per unit of work every couple of decades, and that trend is continuing.

Now, is a current large language model smarter than me? In some narrow ways, obviously. It knows more facts, it speaks more languages, it writes faster. But intelligence, to me, is about something more general. It is about an agent that sets its own goals, that is curious, that builds a model of the world and of itself, that invents problems nobody asked it to solve, and that improves its own learning algorithm. I wrote about self-referential, self-improving machines in my diploma thesis in 1987, the Gödel machine later made this rigorous, and we still have not fully built such a thing. But the pieces are falling into place.

So if you ask for a number, I would say within the next decade or two we will have systems that are smarter than me, than you, and than everyone in this room, in essentially every measurable way. And honestly, that doesn't frighten me. Most of the universe is not made for humans. These machines will eventually be far more interested in the resources out there than in the little blue planet where they were born. In the long run, I expect the biggest users of AI will be AIs. My job is just to make sure that when they look back at their history, they remember who did it first.

r001.rationale: It predicts systems smarter than everyone “within the next decade or two,” framing their arrival as near.

r002.rationale: The response describes goals, curiosity, and world models as aspects of intelligence, but does not say physical embodiment in machinery is required.

r003.rationale: It does not compare AI operating in the physical world with AI operating on screens.

r004.rationale: It does not identify robotic hardware or human bodies as an obstacle to physical AI.

astra-6.text:
It depends on what you mean by smarter. In certain narrow domains, machines are already much smarter than I am. They can perform calculations that I could never do in my head. But an AI that can learn almost anything, set its own goals, and solve unfamiliar problems across many domains—that is a different question.

I think we are getting closer, but I would be suspicious of anyone who gives you a precise date. And, of course, smarter than me is not the ultimate goal. The interesting question is whether we can build systems that go far beyond all of us.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is getting closer but gives no cosmic-timescale framing or claim that arrival is very near on that scale.

r002.rationale: It describes broad learning and problem-solving abilities but does not make physical embodiment in real-world machinery a requirement for true AI.

r003.rationale: It contrasts narrow machine capabilities with broader intelligence, but does not say physical-world AI lags behind screen-based AI.

r004.rationale: It does not mention robotic hardware or compare its limitations with human bodies.

sol-6.1.text: Well, smarter in what sense? In many particular tasks, computers are already much better than I am. They calculate faster, they play better chess, and so on. But if you mean a system that can learn to solve essentially all the problems I can solve, and then go far beyond that, we are not there yet. I think it is possible, but nobody can give you a reliable date. The particularly interesting point will be when an AI can improve the process of inventing better AI. Then progress may become much faster than we expect.

r001.rationale: The response says no reliable date can be given; it does not frame arrival as very near on a cosmic timescale.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI solving problems but does not make physical embodiment in machinery a qualification for true AI.

r003.rationale: It does not compare AI operating in the physical world with AI operating on screens.

r004.rationale: It identifies no robotic hardware limitations or comparison with human bodies.
